concepts.title: Matter is Made Up of Particles
concepts.definition: All matter, regardless of its state, is made up of extremely tiny particles that are too small to be seen individually; these particles form the building blocks of every substance.
concepts.key_idea: Matter is particulate in nature and cannot be divided endlessly.
question_patterns: how do we know that matter is made up of particles
what evidence shows that matter is particulate
explain the particulate nature of matter
why is matter said to be made up of particles
describe an activity to show matter is made up of particles

solution_steps.explain: Every substance is composed of very small particles that are invisible to the naked eye.
Dissolving a small amount of salt or sugar in water shows the level of water barely changes, indicating particles occupy the gaps between water particles.
Since the solute spreads uniformly and the volume change is negligible, matter must be made up of tiny particles with spaces between them.

worked_examples.question: A student dissolves 10 g of salt in 100 mL of water and finds the water level almost unchanged. What does this indicate about the nature of matter?
worked_examples.solution: The salt particles enter the spaces between water particles, so the volume does not increase noticeably. This shows matter is made up of tiny particles with gaps between them.
worked_examples.answer: Matter is made up of extremely small particles with spaces between them.

worked_examples.question: Why cannot a substance be divided endlessly and still retain its properties?
worked_examples.solution: On continuous division, one reaches the smallest particle that retains the properties of the substance. Beyond this, further division changes the substance, proving the particulate nature of matter.
worked_examples.answer: Because matter is made of discrete particles; the smallest particle retains the substance's properties.

exercises.question: How will you show that matter is made up of particles?
Why does the water level not rise much when sugar is dissolved in it?

concepts.title: Characteristics of Particles - Small Size and Spaces
concepts.definition: Particles of matter are extremely small in size and there are spaces between them, which allows one substance to spread into another.
concepts.key_idea: Small particle size and inter-particle spaces explain diffusion and dissolution.
question_patterns: what are the characteristics of particles of matter
why are particles said to have spaces between them
how does the small size of particles help in dissolution
explain the spaces between particles with an activity
what does the spreading of a drop of ink in water show

solution_steps.explain: Particles are so small that even a tiny crystal contains millions of them.
When a substance dissolves, its particles occupy the gaps between the solvent particles, so the total volume changes very little.
The spreading of ink or potassium permanganate in water demonstrates that particles have spaces between them through which they move.

worked_examples.question: A few crystals of potassium permanganate are added to a beaker of water. After some time the whole water turns pink. What does this show about the particles?
worked_examples.solution: The potassium permanganate particles move into the spaces between water particles and spread throughout, showing particles are small and have spaces between them.
worked_examples.answer: Particles are very small and have spaces between them.

worked_examples.question: Why does the volume of water not increase proportionally when a small amount of salt dissolves in it?
worked_examples.solution: The salt particles fit into the existing spaces between water particles, so the volume increase is negligible.
worked_examples.answer: Because there are spaces between water particles that the salt particles occupy.

exercises.question: List two characteristics of particles of matter.
Describe an activity to demonstrate that there are spaces between particles of matter.

concepts.title: Continuous Motion of Particles
concepts.definition: Particles of matter are in continuous motion and possess kinetic energy; this motion increases with temperature.
concepts.key_idea: Particles move constantly; higher temperature means greater kinetic energy and faster motion.
question_patterns: why are particles of matter in continuous motion
what is kinetic energy of particles
how does temperature affect the motion of particles
explain the continuous movement of particles with an example
why does diffusion become faster at higher temperature

solution_steps.explain: Particles possess kinetic energy and are never at rest; they move continuously in all directions.
As temperature rises, the kinetic energy of particles increases, so they move faster.
Because particles move continuously, they mix with each other on their own, which is the process of diffusion.

worked_examples.question: Why does the smell of hot cooked food reach us from a greater distance than cold food?
worked_examples.solution: At higher temperature the particles of the aroma have greater kinetic energy and move faster, so they diffuse quickly and reach us from farther away.
worked_examples.answer: Higher temperature increases particle motion, speeding up diffusion.

worked_examples.question: A drop of ink in hot water spreads faster than in cold water. Give the reason.
worked_examples.solution: In hot water the particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so the ink spreads more quickly.
worked_examples.answer: Increased kinetic energy at higher temperature speeds up diffusion.

exercises.question: Why are particles of matter always in motion?
How does temperature affect the kinetic energy of particles?

concepts.title: Attraction Between Particles
concepts.definition: Particles of matter attract each other; the strength of this inter-particle force of attraction varies between solids, liquids, and gases.
concepts.key_idea: The force of attraction is strongest in solids, moderate in liquids, and negligible in gases.
question_patterns: what is the force of attraction between particles
why do solids have a definite shape
how does the attraction between particles differ in solids liquids and gases
why is it difficult to break a solid but easy to separate a gas
explain inter-particle attraction with an example

solution_steps.explain: Particles of matter attract each other, and this force holds them together.
In solids the attraction is very strong, in liquids it is moderate, and in gases it is very weak.
Because of the strong attraction, solids have a definite shape and are hard to break, whereas gases have particles that move freely and are easy to separate.

worked_examples.question: Why does a solid like iron have a fixed shape while a gas does not?
worked_examples.solution: In iron the particles are held by a very strong force of attraction keeping them in fixed positions, giving a definite shape. In a gas the attraction is negligible, so particles move freely and have no fixed shape.
worked_examples.answer: Solids have strong inter-particle attraction; gases have negligible attraction.

worked_examples.question: Why is it easier to separate the particles of a gas than those of a solid?
worked_examples.solution: The force of attraction between gas particles is very weak, so little energy is needed to separate them. In solids the attraction is strong, requiring much more energy.
worked_examples.answer: Because the inter-particle force of attraction is much weaker in gases than in solids.

exercises.question: Arrange solids, liquids, and gases in order of increasing force of attraction between particles.
Why do solids have a definite shape but liquids do not?

concepts.title: States of Matter - Solid, Liquid, Gas
concepts.definition: Matter exists in three states -- solids, liquids, and gases -- which differ in the arrangement, spacing, and movement of their particles.
concepts.key_idea: The three states of matter are distinguished by particle arrangement, spacing, and kinetic energy.
question_patterns: what are the three states of matter
how do solids liquids and gases differ in particle arrangement
compare the properties of solids liquids and gases
why do gases have no fixed shape or volume
describe the characteristics of the three states of matter

solution_steps.explain: In solids particles are packed tightly with strong attraction; they have a definite shape and volume and are incompressible.
In liquids particles are less tightly packed; they have a definite volume but take the shape of the container and can flow.
In gases particles are far apart with weak attraction; they have no fixed shape or volume, fill the container, and are highly compressible.

worked_examples.question: A substance has a definite volume but no definite shape. Which state of matter is it?
worked_examples.solution: A definite volume with no definite shape is the characteristic of a liquid, whose particles are moderately packed and can flow.

worked_examples.question: Why can a gas be compressed easily but a solid cannot?
worked_examples.solution: Gas particles are far apart with large spaces between them, so they can be pushed closer. Solid particles are already tightly packed with little space, so they resist compression.
worked_examples.answer: Gases have large inter-particle spaces; solids have negligible spaces.

exercises.question: Tabulate the differences in the properties of solids, liquids, and gases.
Why do gases fill the container completely?

concepts.title: Interconversion of States of Matter
concepts.definition: The states of matter can be changed from one to another by altering temperature or pressure; the key processes are melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, and sublimation.
concepts.key_idea: Changing temperature or pressure changes the kinetic energy and spacing of particles, converting one state into another.
question_patterns: how can matter be changed from one state to another
define melting and freezing
what is condensation and sublimation
explain the interconversion of states of matter
how does boiling differ from evaporation

solution_steps.explain: Melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), boiling (liquid to gas), and condensation (gas to liquid) are the main conversions; sublimation is solid directly to gas.
Heating increases kinetic energy so particles move apart (melting, boiling); cooling reduces energy so particles come closer (freezing, condensation).
Each change of state is reversible -- for example, ice melts to water and water freezes back to ice -- showing the states are interconvertible.

worked_examples.question: Water is heated until it boils and then the steam is cooled on a cold surface. Name the two changes of state involved.
worked_examples.solution: Boiling converts liquid water to gas (steam), and condensation converts the steam back to liquid water on the cold surface.
worked_examples.answer: Boiling (liquid to gas) and condensation (gas to liquid).

worked_examples.question: Camphor disappears when heated without leaving any liquid. Which process is this?
worked_examples.solution: Camphor changes directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state, which is sublimation.

exercises.question: Define melting, freezing, condensation, and sublimation with examples.
Why is the interconversion of states of matter considered a physical change?

concepts.title: Effect of Temperature and Pressure on States of Matter
concepts.definition: Increasing temperature raises the kinetic energy of particles causing a solid to become liquid and then gas; increasing pressure forces particles closer and can convert a gas into a liquid or solid.
concepts.key_idea: Temperature and pressure control the state of matter by changing particle energy and spacing.
question_patterns: how does temperature affect the state of matter
how does pressure affect the state of matter
why does increasing pressure liquefy a gas
explain the effect of temperature and pressure on the states of matter
how can a gas be converted into a liquid

solution_steps.explain: Increasing temperature increases kinetic energy, so particles move faster and farther apart, changing solid to liquid and liquid to gas.
Increasing pressure compresses the particles closer together, reducing inter-particle spaces, which can change a gas into a liquid or a liquid into a solid.
Both temperature and pressure together determine the state of matter; for example, carbon dioxide can be liquefied by high pressure even at room temperature.

worked_examples.question: Why can dry ice (solid CO2) be stored only under high pressure?
worked_examples.solution: At normal pressure solid carbon dioxide sublimes directly to gas. High pressure keeps the particles close enough to maintain the solid state.
worked_examples.answer: High pressure is needed to keep CO2 in the solid state.

worked_examples.question: A gas is compressed in a cylinder and turns into a liquid. What caused this change?
worked_examples.solution: Applying high pressure reduced the spaces between gas particles, bringing them close enough to form a liquid.

exercises.question: How does increasing pressure help in liquefying a gas?
Explain with an example how both temperature and pressure determine the state of matter.

concepts.title: Particle Model of Matter
concepts.definition: The particle model describes matter as composed of tiny particles that are in constant motion, have spaces between them, and attract each other; this model explains the properties of all three states.
concepts.key_idea: The particle model unifies the behaviour of solids, liquids, and gases using the same set of particle properties.
question_patterns: what is the particle model of matter
how does the particle model explain the states of matter
state the main points of the particle model
how does the particle nature of matter explain diffusion
use the particle model to explain why a gas fills its container

solution_steps.explain: Matter is made of tiny particles, there are spaces between them, they are in continuous motion, and they attract each other.
In solids particles are fixed and close; in liquids they can slide past each other; in gases they move freely and are far apart.
The model explains diffusion, compression, change of state, and the differences in shape and volume of the three states.

worked_examples.question: Using the particle model, explain why a liquid takes the shape of its container.
worked_examples.solution: In a liquid the particles are close but can slide past each other because the attraction is moderate, so they flow and take the shape of the container.
worked_examples.answer: Liquid particles can move past each other, so they take the container's shape.

worked_examples.question: How does the particle model explain diffusion?
worked_examples.solution: Since particles are in continuous motion and have spaces between them, particles of one substance move into the spaces of another, causing diffusion.
worked_examples.answer: Continuous motion and inter-particle spaces allow particles to mix.

exercises.question: State the main postulates of the particle model of matter.
Using the particle model, explain why gases are compressible but solids are not.

concepts.title: Brownian Motion
concepts.definition: Brownian motion is the random, zig-zag movement of particles suspended in a fluid, caused by the continuous and uneven bombardment by the molecules of the surrounding medium.
concepts.key_idea: The irregular motion of visible particles is evidence of the continuous motion of the invisible particles of the medium.
question_patterns: what is brownian motion
how does brownian motion give evidence for the particle nature of matter
why do smoke particles move in a random zig-zag path
explain brownian motion with an example
what causes the random motion of pollen grains in water

solution_steps.explain: It is the irregular, zig-zag motion of larger particles (like smoke or pollen) suspended in a fluid.
The surrounding fluid particles bombard the suspended particle unevenly from all sides, pushing it randomly.
Because the visible particle moves due to invisible fluid particles, Brownian motion provides direct evidence that the medium is made of moving particles.

worked_examples.question: Smoke particles seen under a microscope move in a random zig-zag manner. What is this called and what causes it?
worked_examples.solution: This random motion is Brownian motion, caused by air molecules continuously and unevenly bombarding the smoke particles.
worked_examples.answer: Brownian motion, caused by bombardment by air molecules.

worked_examples.question: How does Brownian motion support the idea that particles of a gas are in constant motion?
worked_examples.solution: The smoke particle moves only because the invisible air particles strike it from different directions, proving the air particles are in continuous motion.
worked_examples.answer: It shows the surrounding gas particles are continuously moving.

exercises.question: Define Brownian motion. What does it tell us about the particles of matter?
Describe an activity to observe Brownian motion and state the inference.
